summary:
EarthPulse is a web application that helps anyone find out what is changing in the Earth system, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users pick a NASA POWER variable (such as air temperature, solar radiation or precipitation) and a location, using a map click, city search or one-click presets (Sahara, Amazon, Sundarbans, Delhi, Svalbard). The app retrieves monthly data from 1981 to the present (MERRA-2 and CERES) and plots the time series.

It then runs rigorous trend analysis: Theil-Sen slope, Mann-Kendall test, an OLS slope t-test with confidence intervals, and Durbin-Watson diagnostics. The result appears as a plain-language verdict: significant, not significant, or more data needed. Region comparison shows how the same variable can trend in opposite directions in different places. Projections are clearly labelled as conditional, and the app never claims causation.

For students and the public, EarthPulse includes simple definitions, a guided wizard, quizzes, a glossary and Terra, an AI tutor that works offline too. Trend detection is central to understanding climate change, and EarthPulse makes it transparent and accessible, turning NASA data into evidence-based understanding.
details:
What it does and how it works

EarthPulse lets a user pick an Earth-science variable (air temperature, solar radiation, precipitation, humidity and more) and a place on Earth. The place can be chosen by clicking on the map, searching a city, entering coordinates, or loading a preset such as the Sahara Desert, Amazon Rainforest, Sundarbans Estuary, Delhi Megacity or Svalbard Arctic.

The backend fetches monthly NASA POWER data from 1981 to the present (MERRA-2 reanalysis and CERES satellite data) and caches it. The app plots the time series with a rolling mean and a within-year max-min ribbon, then answers four questions in a result card: what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is statistically significant.

Statistical method

  • Theil-Sen slope for a robust rate of change (units per decade, with a 95% confidence interval)
  • Mann-Kendall test, with tie-corrected variance
  • OLS slope t-test, as the challenge suggests
  • Durbin-Watson test for autocorrelation
  • Calendar-day-weighted monthly means. Missing months are never interpolated
  • Strict completeness rules before any trend is tested
  • Conditional projections with Student-t prediction intervals, plus hindcast validation against a naive baseline

The verdict is shown in plain language: significant, not significant, or more data needed. A Compare Regions mode shows the same variable in two places, which highlights that trends can move in opposite directions.

Benefits and intended impact

The target audience is high-school and college students, and curious members of the public. The app turns raw satellite and reanalysis data into evidence-based understanding. It supports this with:

  • Simple variable definitions
  • A guided Trend Detective Wizard
  • Role profiles (Geologist, Physicist, Curious Mind)
  • A glossary and quizzes
  • Terra, an AI tutor that also works offline
  • Auto-generated explainer videos
  • PDF, CSV and PNG exports

The aim is to teach people how scientists decide whether a change is real or just noise.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, SQLite, HTTPX, Pytest (33 unit tests)
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • Visualization: Plotly.js, Leaflet, KaTeX
  • Reports and video: jsPDF, HTML5 Canvas, Web Audio API, Web Speech API
  • Data: NASA POWER API and Open-Meteo geocoding. No API keys are required
  • Deployment: Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend), or Docker

No special hardware is needed. It runs in any modern browser.

Creativity

EarthPulse treats the user as a “data detective” rather than a dashboard viewer. It combines a scientifically rigorous engine with a guided, story-style experience, including generated data-story videos with narration and an AI tutor. It also stays honest about uncertainty.

Factors considered

  • Scientific honesty: no fake causal claims, no black-box forecasts, and clear limitations
  • Accessibility: plain language, tooltips, and a clean, responsive interface
  • Reproducibility: open NASA data, documented methods, and automated tests
  • Reliability: caching, clear error messages for ocean or no-data points, and an offline fallback for the tutor
  • Limitations: the record is monthly and does not cover trends below the grid-cell scale

AI usage: AI coding assistants were used for development support, and this is disclosed in AI_USAGE.md. All data comes from NASA sources, which are cited in SCIENCE-SOURCES.md.
